To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the auditory "learning biographies" of individuals result in multiple and interchangeable representations of music, and that these representations are rapidly adaptable and distributed across both hemispheres of the brain.

(1) music cognition is modular, (2) each of these modules is processed by a network, (3) the networks of each module are distributed in both hemispheries, and (4) the networks of a module vary between individuals, depending on their auditory learning biography

music processing is a highly complex phenomenon, which is not only based on auditory perception, but includes multiple sensory and motor components, and that it involves multiple neuronal networks, including those of both hemispheries, and that these networks are highly variable and rapidly adaptive, reflecting the individual learning biography of the subject.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether and to what extent the brain substrates of musical cognition can be modified by learning, experience, and education.
how the brain processes music and how music processing in the brain is influenced by musical experience.
the question of how the brain processes and represents music.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no conclusive statement on brain substrates for music processing, because music processing is a highly variable phenomenon, which is influenced by multiple, in many cases unknown factors.
there is no conclusive statement on the question of where music processing is located in the brain, as this is highly dependent on individual learning history.
the brain substrates for music are as manifold and variable as music is.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the brain of a professional musician is a music center, and not the right hemisphere.
the human brain is not only a musical machine, but also a musical instrument.
music processing in the brain is modular, but not localized, and that it is shaped by individual experiences.
The main takeaway from our work is that
music processing in the brain is not only a question of "how" but also of "what." (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2019 APA, all rights reserved)
music education can change the brain, but it is not possible to predict the exact outcome of these changes.
the brain is a highly flexible system that adapts to the environment.
